text: Everything so far has worked within one table. Real data engineering almost always means combining two — a lookup table, a reference list, a second export. Merging is pandas' version of a SQL join, and it's the perfect note to close this chapter on.

merge on region, how equals left, is exactly a SQL left join — every row of orders.csv keeps its place and picks up warehouse_city from whichever warehouses row shares its region. All four regions here have a match, so you gain a column and lose nothing — still 20 rows.

A real reference table isn't always this complete. This priority table leaves Accessories out on purpose. A left merge still keeps all 20 rows — it always keeps every row from the left side — it just can't find a match for those 4 Accessories orders, so ship_priority comes back NaN for them.

Switch that same merge to how equals inner, and those 4 unmatched Accessories orders vanish entirely — down from 20 rows to 16. That's the real danger: an inner merge drops rows silently, with no NaN warning sign the way a left join gives you.

Four strategies, one decision: left keeps all of your main data and flags gaps. Inner keeps only confirmed matches. Right is rare — it's just swapping which side you call merge on. And outer keeps everything from both sides, mismatches and all.

That closes out Chapter 4 — you can now load, select, clean, transform, aggregate, and merge real tabular data with pandas. Chapter 5 starts next, connecting Python directly to SQL Server so you can pull real database tables straight into a DataFrame.
